articles.text: Residents interested in running for City Council or Piedmont School Board can pick up nomination documents from the City Clerk by appointment until Friday, August 9. Holy One: As we have celebrated today, you created us in your image, you created us for friendship with you and friendship with one another. We give thanks for the grace, wisdom and integrity that have marked his term in office and their stewardship of the White House. We respect their care for our nation and their patriotic values. In this moment, by faith, we claim these truths for ourselves. These truths celebrate the fact that you have been our help in ages past and are our hope for years to come. articles.text: Photos by Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District A lab technician at the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District administers an oral swab to an expired crow. The lab uses two tests to confirm the presence of West Nile virus. which is measured on a scale of 0 to 640. “When the test returned, it had capped out at the highest possible test value, indicating the highest possible level of disease,” said Pierce. The department went into “instant response” mode on Wednesday, July 10. Lab technicians were dispatched to Dracena Park and set traps at likely mosquito centers within a one-mile radius of Dracena Park, including sewers and bodies of water. Areas where birds congregate were also investigated. An investigation by the Abatement District has not identified any West Nile-positive mosquitoes or West Nile-positive birds in the area. A second test confirmed the bird was positive for West Nile Virus on Tuesday, July 16. Pierce said that it is standard policy for her department to wait until this second test to make any announcements. The City of Piedmont was informed of the situation on Thursday, July 18, and issued a press release the following day. “Abatement District technicians have inspected the area where the bird was found, set mosquito traps, and searched for potential breeding grounds. Public Works staff will continue to coordinate with the Abatement District to review the park for areas of concern and take any recommended preventative actions,” reads the press release. Pierce added that the situation was “very unusual” for Piedmont and that West Nile-positive birds have not been discovered in neighboring towns of Berkeley, Oakland, Emeryville or Albany. The nearest positive case was reported earlier this year in Union City, over 25 miles to the south. This is the first positive bird detected in Piedmont in 2024. When a mosquito infects a bird with West Nile Virus, that bird can spread the disease to other mosquitos in its surrounding area. This process can transmit the virus to other communities when the bird travels. You may now subscribe online at:

Additionally, this is the 19th positive bird discovered in Alameda County this year and the 139th overall in California, a slight increase from the same time last year. In California, no humans have tested positive for West Nile virus this year. What you can do If you see a dead bird, call 1-877-WNV-BIRD or report it online at westnile.ca.gov. Birds are especially vulnerable to West Nile virus and can spread the disease over great distances because of their flight patterns. Mosquito districts throughout the state test dead birds for West Nile virus to track where the virus is spreading. If you have mosquito issues on your property, contact the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District for assistance by calling (510) 783-7744 or filling out an online service request. Be sure to check your backyard for standing water that may have been left by accident. Take precautions to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes. Avoid areas with mosquitoes during the early morning and dusk, when they are most active. Use an EPA-approved insect repellent. If possible, wear long sleeves and long pants to decrease areas where they can bite. West Nile virus is transmitted to people and animals through the bite of an infected mosquito. Most people infected with West Nile virus have no symptoms. Around one in five people infected will develop symptoms such as fever, headache, body aches, joint pains, vomiting, or rash. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will be participating in this year’s National Night Out on Tuesday, August 6, from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m. at several locations in town. National Night Out is an annual community-building event hosted by thousands of communities nationwide who join together with their local police departments to promote public safety. The event is designed to promote police-community partnerships and neighborhood camaraderie to make communities safer. Typically, neighbors spend the evening outside with their neighbors and members of the fire and police departments. Often it is a series of block parties. Three neighborhoods have already confirmed their participation: Glen Alpine-Sotelo, Huntleigh-Lexford, and Waldo and Blair. The Police Department, including Chief Jeremy Bowers and Capt. Chris Monahan will attend all three locations. “I always enjoy what I call ‘non-enforcement contact,’” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “This is an opportunity for us to get out and meet, discuss, share and communicate with people Photo by Piedmont Police Department Officer Jason Germano and Capt. Chris Monahan attend a National Night Out block party on Blair Avenue in 2023. in our community in a non-law enforcement scenario. This is not somebody calling because their car just got burglarized. It’s not somebody who’s getting a ticket for not wearing their seatbelt. These are events where neighbors come together and get the chance to talk to police and fire.” Monahan also extolled the virtues of getting neighbors to meet one another. “On any given shift, PPD has four officers on duty and eight firefighters. In case of a natural disaster where response times are heightened, those neighbors are going to be each others’ first line of support outside of their immediate families.” For more information about hosting or attending a block party, contact PPD Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo at ncasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: City Clerk Anna Brown (left) swears in new firefighter paramedics Viktoriya Franzen, Gary Randolph and Lucas Romero at a July 15 city council meeting. The Piedmont Fire Department welcomed three newly-minted firefighter paramedics at a badge-pinning ceremony during a city council meeting on Monday, July 15. Viktoriya Franzen, Gary Randolph and Lucas Romero completed their training at Las Positas College’s East Bay Regional Fire Academy in Livermore on Saturday, July 13. At the ceremony, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan spoke about the importance of the role. “Every shift, the firefighter paramedic is responsible for ensuring their readiness to respond in addition to that of their apparatus, equipment, and safety gear. You’ll see firefighter medics pulling hose, throwing ladders and providing advanced medical care whenever we respond to emergencies. Teamwork is essential and they need to fit into several roles that can change at any moment on any scene,” said Brannigan. The first to be pinned was Franzen. She and her family emigrated to the United States from Russia 20 years ago. She got her first job at Starbucks in high school, which she credits with developing skills in both teamwork and for making good coffee “which is critical in the firehouse,” joked Brannigan. Franzen spent four years delivering compassionate medical care in San Joaquin County before being hired in Piedmont. Franzen was pinned by her parents Andre and Svetlana Pakhamov. Gary Randolph, who was next to be pinned, was a paramedic for two years in Sonoma County. He worked for three and a half years with an ambulance company and served as a reserve firefighter for one year in Healdsburg. articles.text: For thousands of students that went through Piedmont schools since 1998, a formal and fascinating introduction to science was thanks to Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Greenebaum. He has retired after 31 years of teaching. Greenebaum’s love and enthusiasm for science and life in general will be greatly missed from the school district this fall. Students attending one of Greenebaum’s classes may remember him as a zany, high-energy teacher, always quick to recite a clever rhyme to help students recall a scientific principal. “I’m a musical guy. I’m always singing. I’ve got a song in my heart all the time,” said Greenebaum. “I found that singing classroom management expectations is better than harping on kids every day. ‘Sit down, get out your stuff.’ So then I developed these songs,” he said. Those daily expectation began with the backpack song. “Boom, boom, boom, boom, please put those backpacks...Under the tables, leaving the aisles clear.” To which students in class replied back “Cha, cha, cha.” Greenebaum underscored the importance of accurate data collection by starting every class off by also singing “Get that data, down!” He coined the phrase in his first teaching post in Minneapolis; data points for his eighth grade class included values for sunrise, sunset, temperature and phases of the moon. Ted Greenebaum’s teaching career: • 1993-1998 – Minneapolis Public School science • 1998-2024 – Piedmont Middle School science For many people, the middle school years are notoriously difficult and hard to understand, but Greenebaum’s enthusiasm and energy famously worked for students. His zeal for science and for the natural world provided comic relief without self-apprehension, a refreshing foil to the entropy and chaos underway during those formidable years. “I am fascinated by life. I’m fascinated by science and the world and the human condition. And in those three years of middle school, sixth, seventh, and eighth grade, it’s the most dynamic time in a person’s life. Eighth graders [are] probably PMS science teacher Ted Greenebaum dressed up as Elvis while serving as a judge in the Airbands competition in 2024. Ted Greenebaum, an avid bass fisherman, with a recent catch in his home state of Wisconsin. the most complex animals on the planet,” Greenebaum said. “Eighth graders start that abstract reasoning, and they start to move out of the concrete,” he continued. “They hear in new ways and actually start thinking in a layered way, and are able to process information and reflect on it and speak about it.” Greenebaum speaks with pride of his past students, but really lights up when speaking of his own children. Daughter Zoe Torok, a PHS graduate in 2019 and an All-league athlete in lacrosse, has since received a computer science degree from the University of Chicago and now works for the Pittsburgh Pirates doing data analytics and app development. Greenebaum’s son Oliver will be a PHS senior next year and is a talented fencer. Ted Greenebaum with fellow PMS teacher Anjuna Lohnes preparing for search and rescue training in 2023. Greenebaum’s long and successful career began with the same conviction he utilized every day in the classroom. After teaching for five years in the state of Minnesota in the 1990s, Greenebaum and his wife Melissa decided to move somewhere warmer, where snow in May was not possible. Greenebaum saw an ad in the San Francisco Chronicle for a Piedmont Middle School Science Teacher while he was on the west coast looking for jobs. “I went down there on Memorial Day Monday [in May of 1998], to the district office and I banged on the door with my portfolio, and the assistant superintendent, Patrick Gemma, was there working. He was the only soul there. I came in, and I just evidently blew him away,” recalled Greenebaum. Greenebaum talked with PMS Principal John Morrison, and was hired shortly after. “I’m going to take time for myself for sure, and I’m also going to get back to helping others and helping improve the world, on my time, not on someone else’s time,” he said of retirement. Greenebaum also wanted to express how much he appreciated the opportunity to teach in Piedmont. “It’s a wonderful place to live and teach, and the experiences I’ve had and the people I’ve met have been wonderful and supportive. I wish more places had the resources that the Piedmont community has, and I wish that more places had the attitude towards education that Piedmont has,” he said. articles.text: Anybody at any age can be a scientist or an expert observer. Scientists make keen observations to help them understand why things are the way they are. This leads them to form and test educated guesses, paving the way for discoveries. It all starts with observation, a skill that we can practice in our everyday lives. Believe it or not, it’s easy and fun to do. One way to enjoy practicing observations is through nature journaling. It’s like keeping a journal, but instead of writing about your day, you use your senses to notice the amazing things around you. All you need is paper and something to write or draw with. Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you. Can you hear cars honking or the wind blowing? Jot down or sketch what you hear. Next, close your eyes, take a few deep breaths, and experience the scents around you, like trees or flowers. Then, write down your smell observations. Taste is closely tied to our sense of smell. Take a moment to notice any lingering tastes in your mouth, like breakfast or toothpaste. It’s worth journaling about. For touch, feel free to stand up and move around, exploring objects gently with your hands. Note the differences and use your nature journal to document your observations through writing or drawing. Finally, what can you see with your eyes? Humans depend greatly on our sense of sight, so this last section may bring you many things to write about. When you’ve finished, you will have a page of observations that paint a picture across all senses. When you try nature journaling again, you can look back, compare how each day looks different, and notice how each time you practice observations you get better at it, bit by bit. articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. PART FIVE Though we didn’t advertise it, Jordie and I loved to read, and there was no place better for reading than the Watson library, a terrific old brick and timber building with lots of columns and wide concrete steps, leading up to tall oak doors with all this fancy glass that was so thick it looked like the bottom of a coke bottle. Just inside those doors sat Mrs. Hightower, the librarian. She was a straight-backed, serious lady who hardly ever smiled, just sort of puckered her lips like she was considering a smile and decided against it. Mrs. Hightower was usually seated at an elevated desk, her lookout post, and when we walked by she would watch us, her dark eyes flashing behind silver wire-rimmed glasses, like she was certain we had a bunch of overdue books hidden under our beds at home. Once, though, when I glanced back, I saw her smiling, sort of, and decided she was actually happy to see us. Jordie and I never really talked much about the books we read and no one ever asked. It was just something we did. But while the library was like our personal secret, going to the movies was just the opposite. Our house was only a short bike ride to the Vista Theater where every Saturday afternoon they had a special matinee. If Jordie and I could scrounge up a dollar between us, we’d take our favorite spot up in the balcony, front row, popcorn or Milk Duds in hand, counting the minutes, waiting for the next Republic adventure serial to begin. Like Don Winslow of the Navy. Don was always chasing men in baggy double-breasted suits, wearing fezzes and packing heat. You’d see Don, in a tux no less, hanging off the back of a racing speedboat with no one steering, slugging it out with two or three bad guys with thick, black mustaches, while this terrific looking woman with long silver-blonde hair, wearing a silky nightclub dress and lots of jewelry, is sitting up front, all terrified. Of course, she’s right next to the steering wheel, staring ahead at this approaching tanker, and then down at the wheel like she wasn’t sure what it was for. Meanwhile, Don’s getting punched pretty good and the kids in the theater are going crazy. There was always some kid down front who’d yell, “Grab the wheel, lady!” And everyone’d cheer. But just as the speedboat was about to crash into the tanker, the screen would flash the words: TO BE CONTINUED. And every kid in the theater would let out a groan and swear on a stack of bibles to be back next Saturday, same time, same seat. Of course, everyone knew that Don would escape; we just didn’t know how. While the Republic serials were exciting, there were some movies that turned the old Vista Theater into church, the squirming, squirrelly congregation suddenly quiet, no one wanting to get up for anything, not even more candy. Like The Thing, all about this ten-foot alien that had crashed in a flying saucer at the North Pole, and then escaped from the ice and was wandering around this scientific-military installation doing some serious damage. No one knew where the creature was or even what it was – except it was out there in the storm, killing men and sled dogs, then sucking out their blood, or standing behind some closed door that one of the research guys was trying to open. Lots of kids walked out of the Vista on those days covered with goose bumps, wondering how much furniture they could push in front of their closet doors when they hit the sack that night. Scary or not, the only thing that could keep Jordie and me out of a matinee on a Saturday was Howard, who would give himself a migraine trying to think up chores for us to do, saying how it built character, and how going to the movies was a waste of time and money. Howard Oakely was his full name and he’d come to live with us about a year after our father left. Jordie and I didn’t know what to make of him when our mom brought him home the first time. We stood awkwardly in the living room feeling pretty strange and a little embarrassed. He’d come right from work wearing a starched white shirt with a black leather clip-on bow tie. We learned later that he worked at Sid’s Tire and Motor. He was their window man, the guy who carried a clipboard and took down information and scheduled appointments for people when they called on the phone or brought in their cars. If you had a bad tire or your engine was barely running, Howard became this very important person in your life. PART SIX It didn’t take us long to understand that what kept Howard going were those moments of power. He was the guy. Jordie and me, we’d been down to Sid’s and seen people come in with this look on their faces, like Howard had one of their relatives locked up in a basement somewhere, and they’d just stopped in to drop off the ransom. See, Howard could keep the family Chevy for a couple more days or he could grant parole. You could tell: he loved every minute of it. Howard was a wiry guy with greasy, thinning brown hair that he continually pushed back off his forehead. He smelled of hair cream and cigarettes and usually had a matchstick wedged in the corner of his mouth. The day before he moved in with us, our mom explained how she’d worked out this living arrangement with Howard. One that would benefit everyone, meaning she would have help with the rent and Jordie and I would have a man around the house. Well, we understood the rent part. articles.text: Photos courtesy of WeLoveCycling.com Tadej Pogačar has won his third Tour de France at just 25-years-old. Tadej Pogačar just put himself into the realm of legends as one of the greatest cyclists, winning the 2024 Tour de France. his third Yellow Jersey at age 25. He becomes the first threetime winner since Chris Froome accomplished the feat from 2015 to 2017. Pogačar, s now one victory away from matching Froome and France’s Jacques Anquetil (1957, 1961-1964), and two shy of Spain’s Miguel Indurain (1991- 1995), French great Bernard Hinault (1978-1979, 1981-1982, 1985), and Belgium legend Eddie Merckx (1969-1972, 1974). Stepping into the history books, Pogačar’s run has some similarities to Hinault’s threetour victories in 1981, 1982, and 1985. 1983 and 1984 were won by fellow Frenchman Laurent Fignon. Similarly, Pogačar won in 2020 and 2021 before Jonas Vingegaard won the next two years, This time, the Slovenian took the general classification lead on Stage 4 and never relinquished control, winning six of the race’s 21 stages. He won the final three stages of this year’s tour in miraculous fashion, including the critical Stage 21 time trial—clocking 45:24 on the 33.7 km course, one minute and three seconds ahead of second-place Vingegaard. Pogačar has now won 17 Tour de France stages already in his brief career. “I’m super happy. I cannot describe how happy I am after two hard years in the Tour de France. This year everything was perfection,” Pogačar said This year’s tour also meant history for Biniam Girmay, the first cyclist of African descent to win the points classification and the Green Jersey. Girmay won Stage 3 to become the first African rider to ever win a Tour de France stage, then followed up with wins in Stage 8 and Stage 12. With 387 points, Girmay finished 33 points ahead of second-place Jasper Philipsen who was hoping to win his second consecutive Green Jersey. “I feel like I’m floating through the sky. It’s super nice. I just want to say for the young kids, keep working hard and everything is possible,” Girmay said/ On the local level, Walnut Creek native and Team Visma rider, Matteo Jorgenson, finished in the top-10 of the general classification standings in 8th place. At 25-years-old, the Bay Area star still has years of opportunity ahead. The 112th edition of the Tour de France in 2025 is in development with the first three stages already announced, including the Grand Départ in Lille on July 5. Photo courtesy of Team Visma Walnut Creek’s Matteo Jorgenson finished 8th in this year’s Tour de France. He’s Jonas Vingegaard’s teammate on Team Visma.

articles.text: California is famous worldwide for its beauty, romance, and history. The great travel writer Richard Halliburton extolled these in his book “Marvels of the World.” He noted our two great bridges in particular. He did not venture south to the Monterey Peninsula. We did it in order to attend some concerts at the Carmel Bach Festival. First, it’s an adventure just getting there. You can take the coast route or you can go through the mountains or you can go directly south through the farmlands of the Salinas Valley. These days, it’s a good idea to check what the traffic is like in advance. The best bet seems to be through Salinas Valley, but you guessed it. — the traffic was horrendous. We stopped off at the Jellyfish Restaurant in Gilroy for a marvelous lunch. The restaurant is owned by Chinese immigrants, but the restaurant specializes in Louisiana seafood, Our lunch consisted of a gigantic, softshell crab Poboy with French fries and a side order of fried okra. When the food arrived, it was enough for an army. And delicious too. Our friendly waiter advised us to proceed on the back roads and avoid the highway because of the bumper-to-bumper traffic. But the traffic was bad no matter where we went. Richard Halliburton would’ve found a beautiful way to describe an unfortunate situation. That was the beauty of his writing. We arrived in the sparkling gem of a city that is Carmel. There are colorful shops and good restaurants everywhere. There is not a traffic light anywhere in the city. Our first concert at the festival was devoted to the gospel of John as envisioned by Johann Sebastian Bach in his St. John’s Passion. It was first performed on Good Friday in the year 1724. What a coincidence that this is the 300th anniversary of that performance. This was as close to an opera as Johann Sebastian Bach ever got. It was his intention to get the audience emotionally involved. He was successful to say the least. This performance, as conducted by Grete Pedersen, with vocal soloists, chorus and orchestra featured a multilingual version of this masterpiece. This was logical because when God speaks to humanity it is through telepathy in any language the individual speaks. Some have criticized the St. John’s Passion because of its seeming antisemitism. While some people might see this as a fault, Bach handled it well, and the conclusion is that we shall have peace. The Bach Festival has been in Carmel since 1935 and has been successful over those many years. Music Directors are in place for long periods of time. Management is excellent, and all of the musicians are inspired. The conductor Grete Pederson is now in her second year as music Director. As a conductor, she has a clear, concise beat, and she communicates to all of the musicians in a superior manner. I spoke with some friends in the Orchestra, and they said they enjoy working with her. In addition to her high level of musicianship, she is also an excellent diplomat. The performance maintained a dynamic tension at all times. Photos by Joseph Gold Conductor Grete Pedersen speaks to the audience at the Carmel Bach Festival. the Carmel Bach Festival.

articles.text: One of the many Paleolithic cave paintings found in the Chauvet cave in the Ardeche region of France In 1994, three spelunkers – Jean-Marie Chauvet, Eliette Deschamps and Christian Hillaire – were exploring cliffs in the Ardeche region of France. Feeling an air current, they dug and then crawled into what would become known as the Chauvet cave. Holding a lantern high above her head, and seeing the walls, we’re told, Dechamps yelled back, “They were here.” Who “they” were is soon made evident: cave artists, standing in the Chauvet cave 30,000 years ago, charcoal in hand, drawing some of the most astonishing images imaginable. Paintings that today would be judged remarkable. What the interior of the cave must have been like then can only be imagined: the floor covered with the detritus from cave bears, the walls illuminated by the dim light of fires. Cave of Forgotten Dreams, directed and narrated by Werner Herzog, reveals more than 100 paintings of lions, galloping horses, massive bears, wooly mammoths, a pride of lions, and red handprints on ethereal walls, all left behind by Paleolithic travelers, declarative images and an immortal record of their view of their world. When the discovery by the trio was made known, the French government closed the cave, fearful that even the exhalation of visitors would contaminate the treasures enclosed. Access to the cave is now limited to archeologists and curators, and, as we see, Werner Herzog, who, in 2010, received permission from the French government to film, for a limited time, using specially designed equipment, its interior. What is remarkable, and central to the meaning of this discovery, and to the film, is the quality of the paintings and the astonishing talent of the artists. articles.text: Planes: Fire & Rescue is a nice fit for kids 8-years-old and below and would be an ideal follow-up to Disney’s animated Planes. Both star Dusty Crophopper (Dane Cook). It was in Planes that Dusty realized his dream of becoming a world-class, hotdogging air racer and an international celebrity, basking in the continual attention of the cameras. But then, unexpectedly, as Planes: Fire & Rescue begins, Dusty discovers that his gearbox is failing, the parts he needs to fix it aren’t available, so he can’t reach those top speeds that have allow him to win races. An additional problem is that his much loved hometown airport, Propwash Junction, needs a serious updating. Its equipment is failing to meet compliance. But the situation gives Dusty something to do. He has been yearning to become an aerial firefighter, and so gets certified by the crusty, cranky Blade Ranger (Ed Harris) who is in charge of training. He finds Dusty a bit impulsive but approves him for the Piston Peak squadron. And so begins the story of planes zooming fire ravaged canyons, up into billowing clouds of smoke, swooping down to scoop up water from lakes and rivers, and dropping pink fire retardant. All of them are flying by the seat of their ailerons. Members of the Piston Peakers are risking their lives to protect those on the ground, which includes the ATV smoke jumpers, a courageous bunch who drop out of airplanes, parachute to the ground, and fight the raging fires. The hotshot crew of Piston Peak also includes military transport Cabbie (Dale Dye), and Lil’ Dipper (Julie Bowen), who has a crush on Dusty. And there’s May Day (Hal Holbrook), a dated fire and rescue truck, plus Windlifter (Wes Studi), whose helicopter blades are painted like feathers. One of the squadron’s missions turns out to be an all-handson-deck attempt to save the Grand Fusel Lodge and its guests. Dusty, of course, must overcome his fear as he confronts the ultimate villain in the story, the unforgiving forest fires wjhich are bearing down on the lodge. There’s lots of action, and Dusty manages to get out of some tight spots, as does the Piston Peak squadron. Sure there is peril, but parents shouldn’t be concerned. In spite of the close calls, no one gets hurt. And the little guys will love Dusty’s courageous antics. Planes: Fire & Rescue. Directed by Bob Gannaway. Disney Studios animation. Voiced by Dane Cook, Ed Harris, Dale Dye, Julie Bowen. 1 hr. 23 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Fandango, prime, Disney+/apple tv. A scene from Disney’s Planes: Fire & Rescue

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group was surprised on July 17th as it assembled at the Exedra for its weekly walk. A crew of tree removal workers with a tall crane were in the process of cutting down a big redwood tree behind City Hall. The walkers didn’t know why the tree was being removed. It turned out to be a harbinger of what they were going to see later. Real estate development has long been part of Piedmont’s history. Walter Blair built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 to attract potential residents. Early 20th Century developer Frank C. Havens created Piedmont Park to promote his Piedmont real estate, and currently there is a controversy regarding the development of a lot on Wistaria Way. Going to it would also let the walkers go through Havens’ beautiful neighborhood of Wildwood Gardens. This neighborhood was the site of Havens’ “Wildwood Estate.” He was born into a prominent New York family and after a year in the China shipping trade, he came to San Francisco in 1866 and worked in banking. In about 1880 he founded a stock brokerage before creating the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” in 1895 with F. M. “Borax” Smith. Havens became a major real estate developer in Oakland, Berkeley and Piedmont. Havens and Smith built the Claremont Hotel, and the Syndicate was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It also accumulated at least 13,000 acres of hilltop land that stretched from near Mills College to the boundary of North Berkeley. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road and built his “Wildwood” estate on it. The walkers made their way through the loops that make up Wildwood Gardens and found the back of 101 Wildwood Gardens, Havens’ mansion. Only a portion of it could be seen, but an “H” in the wrought iron gate indicated its origin. The group continued through the upper portion of Wildwood Gardens, past an impressive children’s treehouse with Wildwood Creek running nearby to the seldom-visited Wistaria Way. They made their way up the loop to the lot where another tree removal crew had just cut down many coastal oaks and other trees. This lot was once part of a home, but was donated to a local church after the owner’s death. The land was sold in 2022. The new owners twice submitted applications in 2022 to build a single family home on the lot, but were rejected both times after neighbors and the City objected to the size of the proposed project. The owners then developed a project to divide the lot into two parcels with a plan to construct two new homes on them with an ADU alongside one. This is allowed under a new California law based upon Senate Bill 9 (known as SB9). It went into effect on January 1, 2022, and is intended to address California’s housing shortage by allowing homeowners to divide their lots and build up to four houses on a single-family parcel. This Wistaria project’s application was approved by the Piedmont Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits were approved on July 2, and neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on July 5. A group of them is questioning the project’s legality. They maintain that the lot is protected wetland, as Wildwood Creek traverses it, and the project endangers the wetlands, so it should not be eligible to be split. The City disagrees. The neighbors met with City staff on July 5 and voiced their concerns to the Piedmont City Council at multiple Council meetings, but tree removal began on July 16. The walkers viewed the lot, took a group photo and finished the Wistaria loop. They continued on to Woodland Way, Lafayette and Crocker Avenues and returned to the Exedra with new knowledge of Frank C. Havens and California real estate law. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. and everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. Register at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. A large turnout of 47 walkers and two K-9 best friends participated in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok This month’s favored recipe is for a tasty Apricot Vanilla Cobbler, perfect for warm summer nights. My neighbor’s apricot tree is having a bumper crop this year. And lucky for me, there are several large branches filled with fruit and growing on my side of our fence! They are just about ready to harvest, and even with sharing with our voracious Piedmont squirrels there will be enough to enjoy for our upcoming barbeque. This rustic dessert is a delightful way to highlight summer’s fresh fruit bounty. Here, we’re featuring apricots, but any stone fruit will be equally delicious. Bake this early in the day for your summer BBQ table. Apricot Vanilla Cobbler Makes one 9-inch pan A few advance tips • Make sure the butter and heavy cream are well chilled. You can also pre-chill the mixing bowl in the freezer if your kitchen is warm. • Warm kitchen hack: Place your working bowl in a larger one filled with an inch or two of iced water. This will help prevent the butter from melting. Soft/melty butter = flat, dense topping. • Avoid using really soft apricots as they will turn to mush during the 45 minutes of baking. • Keep the balls of dough on the smaller side, and don’t overcrowd them. This allows for steam to escape from the bubbling apricots and ensures the dough will bake thoroughly too. Walkers examine Wistaria Way development By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group was surprised on July 17th as it assembled at the Exedra for its weekly walk. A crew of tree removal workers with a tall crane were in the process of cutting down a big redwood tree behind City Hall. The walkers didn’t know why the tree was being removed. It turned out to be a harbinger of what they were going to see later. Real estate development has long been part of Piedmont’s history. Walter Blair built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 to attract potential residents. Early 20th Century developer Frank C. Havens created Piedmont Park to promote his Piedmont real estate, and currently there is a controversy regarding the development of a lot on Wistaria Way. Going to it would also let the walkers go through Havens’ beautiful neighborhood of Wildwood Gardens. This neighborhood was the site of Havens’ “Wildwood Estate.” He was born into a prominent New York family and after a year in the China shipping trade, he came to San Francisco in 1866 and worked in banking. In about 1880 he founded a stock brokerage before creating the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” in 1895 with F. M. “Borax” Smith. Havens became a major real estate developer in Oakland, Berkeley and Piedmont. Havens and Smith built the Claremont Hotel, and the Syndicate was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It also accumulated at least 13,000 acres of hilltop land that stretched from near Mills College to the boundary of North Berkeley. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road and built his “Wildwood” estate on it. The walkers made their way through the loops that make up Wildwood Gardens and found the back of 101 Wildwood Gardens, Havens’ mansion. Only a portion of it could be seen, but an “H” in the wrought iron gate indicated its origin. The group continued through the upper portion of Wildwood Gardens, past an impressive children’s treehouse with Wildwood Creek running nearby to the seldom-visited Wistaria Way. They made their way up the loop to the lot where another tree removal crew had just cut down many coastal oaks and other trees. This lot was once part of a home, but was donated to a local church after the owner’s death. The land was sold in 2022. The new owners twice submitted applications in 2022 to build a single family home on the lot, but were rejected both times after neighbors and the City objected to the size of the proposed project. The owners then developed a project to divide the lot into two parcels with a plan to construct two new homes on them with an ADU alongside one. This is allowed under a new California law based upon Senate Bill 9 (known as SB9). It went into effect on January 1, 2022, and is intended to address California’s housing shortage by allowing homeowners to divide their lots and build up to four houses on a single-family parcel. This Wistaria project’s application was approved by the Piedmont Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits were approved on July 2, and neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on July 5. A group of them is questioning the project’s legality. They maintain that the lot is protected wetland, as Wildwood Creek traverses it, and the project endangers the wetlands, so it should not be eligible to be split. The City disagrees. The neighbors met with City staff on July 5 and voiced their concerns to the Piedmont City Council at multiple Council meetings, but tree removal began on July 16. The walkers viewed the lot, took a group photo and finished the Wistaria loop. They continued on to Woodland Way, Lafayette and Crocker Avenues and returned to the Exedra with new knowledge of Frank C. Havens and California real estate law. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. and everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. articles.text: Piedmont native Evan Epstein contracted an aggressive and rare form of cancer and passed away just five weeks after being diagnosed at UCSF in San Francisco. He died on July 5, 2024 at age 42, one week before his 43rd birthday. Born Evan Joel Epstein on July 22, 1981, he was the son of Janet and George Epstein. He graduated from Piedmont High School in 2000, where he loved playing sports, including tennis, golf, swimming, and running cross-country. His two passions were basketball, which he was a member of the Piedmont High School varsity team, and later in his adult life, playing softball on Temple Isaiah’s team in the Sunday Jewish League. He loved fitness and cardio, and was unusually strong even at an early age. Evan graduated from the University of California at Santa Barbara with a Bachelor of Science degree. He did his post-graduate studies at Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, where he received an MBA as well as a Master’s degree in Engineering Management. After college he was a Senior Manager Customer Success for five-plus years at Workday in Pleasanton. He touched countless lives with his easy-going nature and warmth. He had a sarcastic sense of humor to which people could relate. Evan met his lovely wife Katelyn as members of a coed softball league on the Peninsula. It was a good match, with Katelyn an extrovert and Evan’s quiet and Evan Epstein died on July 5, 2024. strong demeanor. They were married in 2016 in Pleasanton. They first lived in Redwood City, and after a few years decided to move to the East Bay. They chose the peaceful Town of Moraga to settle, where they raised two rambunctious boys, Drew and Aaron. Evan was a very “hands on” father, and when Katelyn traveled for work as a Clinical Account Manager for Insightec, he had no qualms about being a stay-at-home dad, while working remotely from home. Evan is survived by his wife Katelyn, his two sons Drew, age 5, and Aaron, age 3. He also leaves his mother, Janet, and father, George, along with sisters Alison Cohen (Eitan) of Los Angeles, and Leah Epstein of Oakland, in-laws Don and Shannon Mosbacher, and numerous other family members. articles.text: In addition to the more prominent architectural styles we have been discussing during the last months, there are yet more to be seen walking through town. Some, like Victorian, are well known but not numerous here; others are hybrid, sometimes difficult to classify. But it also strikes me that every new building, or even every remodel, is necessarily advancing, albeit in small steps, the evolution of any and every base style employed. Looking back maybe 50 years from now, these incremental trends will probably be clearer and help describe how and why the future style came to be. To better understand the initial selection and continuing evolution of building styles it might be helpful to review the process architects normally employ in design. Based on my experience, there are three overriding considerations in the design of any building: the site, the building program, and the design style. 1. Any building site has a specific size, solar orientation, topography, along with existing amenities (like views, trees, rock outcroppings, or water features for example). Any site is also a part of a surrounding context – anything from vacant land to 2-story homes to 12-story office buildings. 2. The building program answers the questions: how big is the intended building? What types of uses and spaces are included? What service systems are included? While zoning regulations limit these options, there still are a wide range of choices based on user lifestyle preference, cost, and response to the site. 3. The design style chosen, no matter how closely or loosely followed, determines the aesthetic of both the building massing and details – inside and out. It influences materials, forms and siting. articles.text: it was a stretch for our mom each month. It was the man around the house part that we had a problem with. As far as we were concerned, there was only one man we wanted around the house and that was our dad and we said so. “Boys,” she said, taking a deep breath, “try and understand. Your father… he just can’t be with us right now. It’s been almost a year and…” Her eyes were welling up with tears and we knew it wasn’t easy for her, saying any of it. “He… well, he may not come back to us.” Jordie stood very still, listening, his body rigid, shaking his head back and forth, saying, “No way, mom. No way. Dad’s coming back. He is. It hasn’t been that long. It hasn’t.” His voice was trembling and he’d begun to cry, trying not to, rubbing his nose with the back of his hand, his cheeks wet, his lower lip quivering with feeling and hurt. I stood close to him, holding my breath, afraid if I said even one word I’d start crying, too, my chest tight and my throat feeling closed off. The thing of it was, Jordie and I had held onto the belief that our dad was coming back so tight our hearts ached, and the thought of having to let go was nearly impossible. Never theless, Howard Oakely arrived early the next morning, it was a Saturday, and he had barely unpacked his suitcase when he set up his tools in our garage along with this 1949 Ford which he made clear was one bang-up set of wheels, a classic, that he was in the process of restoring, “From the ground up,” as he liked to say. From the kitchen window we watched him back it down our driveway and into the garage and went out to see what was up. Howard was standing next to the car, holding a rag, rubbing the front fender with the kind of tenderness you reserved for newborn babies. The object of his affection was a black coupe convertible, one rear fender covered with gray primer, the paint faded on the hood, the chrome bumpers pitted and dull. “Fellas, this here is my pride and joy. This little sweetheart’s gonna be a showstopper when I’m through with ‘er.” Jordie said later that the only thing that wreck was going to stop was traffic when it stalled in an intersection. It was then that Howard declared the garage, meaning our garage, our dad’s garage, to be no-man’s land, and we were told, in what he referred to as “No uncertain terms,” to stay out. He even spelled the word, O-U-T. Very sharp, Howard. “See boys, this here is now my work space.” Emphasis on my. “And I need to know I can spread out and not worry my tools will get messed with. Can’t abide my tools being messed with. You both got the message?” He said all of this while he had one hand on the fender of the Ford, his voice flat, with Texas somewhere in it. “The tools, the car, everything’s off limits. Do not touch. I catch you foolin’ with my stuff, you and me, we’ll have words. We clear about this?” We could tell right away that Howard had a way with kids. Truly. So, having been evicted, we parked our bikes in the back yard and if it rained and we remembered, we put them in the small tool shed. Howard never asked us what we were doing or where we’d been. I don’t think he really cared, as long as we didn’t bother him. The deal with Howard, if he wasn’t in the garage breaking a sweat over the mysteries of the spark plug, he was in the family room slumped deep in his brown-green-yellow vinyl Barcalounger, a big easy chair that had arrived when he did. Jordie called it the barfolounger because of its pukey color. Howard would slump down deep, his feet on the raised foot-rest, watching television, mostly wrestling, drinking what he called the working man’s tranquilizer: a long neck bottle of beer and a shot glass filled with Wild Turkey. Neither of us could see what our mom saw in the guy, but then there are a lot of things that adults do that seem like this huge mystery to kids. articles.text: springs or “take the waters.” To get a feel for the importance of the hotel we must look a little further back. In 1852 Walter Blair bought much of the land in what is now the Piedmont area from the U.S. government. His 600-acre purchase cost him $1.25 per acre, meaning he bought nearly all of Piedmont for $750. The discovery of sulfur spring waters drew other investors towards the area. and they formed the Piedmont Land Company which purchased land around the springs. They sold bonds to build the Piedmont Springs Hotel, hoping to bring in visitors from San Francisco and Oakland. The springs contained sulphur, magnesia, iodine, and iron; bathing in them was (and still is) used to treat ailments such as rheumatism, poor circulation, pain and skin conditions. The hotel was a charming two-story Victorian building surrounded by a wide veranda and second floor balcony. In addition to 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites upstairs, four cottages were later added. The Piedmont Historical Society recalls the hotel’s “Five dining rooms offered the finest food. The main dining room had a crystal chandelier, fine china and velvet drapes and seated thirty-five. Paintings covered the walls.” The Grand Saloon, exclusively for men, featured a billiard table, sophisticated mahogany bar, spittoons and a pot-belly stove in the corner. Marker 2: Piedmont Springs Hotel Opening in 1872, the Piedmont Springs Hotel hosted visitors who came to Piedmont to soak (and drink) from the park’s mineral Piedmont Park’s History Trail Markers Part 2: Piedmont Springs Hotel springs or “take the waters.” To get a feel for the importance of the hotel we must look a little further back. In 1852 Walter Blair bought much of the land in what is now the Piedmont area from the U.S. government. His 600-acre purchase cost him $1.25 per acre, meaning he bought nearly all of Piedmont for $750. The discovery of sulfur spring waters drew other investors towards the area. and they formed the Piedmont Land Company which purchased land around the springs. They sold bonds to build the Piedmont Springs Hotel, hoping to bring in visitors from San Francisco and Oakland. The springs contained sulphur, magnesia, iodine, and iron; bathing in them was (and still is) used to treat ailments such as rheumatism, poor circulation, pain and skin conditions. The hotel was a charming two-story Victorian building surrounded by a wide veranda and second floor balcony. In addition to 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites upstairs, four cottages were later added. The Piedmont Historical Society recalls the hotel’s “Five dining rooms offered the finest food. The main dining room had a crystal chandelier, fine china and velvet drapes and seated thirty-five. Paintings covered the walls.” The Grand Saloon, exclusively for men, featured a billiard table, sophisticated mahogany bar, spittoons and a pot-belly stove in the corner. The hotel drew affluent people from the area as the weather was more favorable to that of San Francisco. Visitors enjoyed the trails to the springs and fine dining coming from Blair’s local dairy and on-site garden. Equestrian enthusiasts frequented the hotel and helped develop a formidable stable across the street where The Piedmont Community Church now stands. The hotel was placed at the end of Piedmont’s main street, Vernal Avenue (now Highland), at the site of the Exedra (Blue Vase). Blair co-owned a public transportation service of horses pulling railway cars from downtown Oakland to Broadway. He developed another horse line from Piedmont Avenue to the The Piedmont Springs Hotel was a tourist destination in the years before the city of Piedmont was incorporated. hotel. All were timed with the ferry crossings to San Francisco in the morning and evening. James Gamble served as proprietor of the Hotel and is credited in naming the region Piedmont. In an advertisement for the hotel, Gamble said, “carriages from San Francisco can make Piedmont, via the Oakland Ferry, in about an hour from Pacific Street wharf.” Travel times have not changed much in 150 years. Large “finger board” signs all along the carriage route marked the way to Piedmont around Lake Merritt. The hotel had a good run of 20 years and was instrumental in the development of Piedmont as a residential community, with guests being enticed to buy large estates up to 20 acres. In 1891 women of Piedmont led a prohibitionist movement to stop the sale of alcohol at the hotel with a petition to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors. The next year the hotel caught fire when sparks from the chimney lit the roof on fire. A fire engine coming from Oakland took two hours to get there, leaving residents and guests to sit and watch it burn down without their own fire department. SAM SHELBY Football, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2025 Sam Shelby is entering an important senior year on the football and track teams. He was named by the SF Chronicle as a candidate for Player of the Year in the East Bay region and to the All-Metro first-team. He was also named to The Mercury News’ All-Bay Area News Group second-team. He helped Piedmont’s football team compile a 7-4 record in the school’s full return to the WACC. He was named the Shoreline Division’s Player of the Year after recording 63 receptions, averaging an eye-popping 17.7 yards per catch for 1,117 yards and 14 touchdowns. He also had 403 rushing yards and averaged 12.2 yards per carry for eight more touchdowns. As the team’s kicker, he also converted 30 point after attempts. Shelby is entering the fall football season with a full head of steam after missing the track season last spring. What is your workout program this summer? I am training with the football team Monday–Thursday from 4:00 to 7 p.m. as well as doing my own personal workouts off the field on weekends. What are your fitness goals for the summer? This summer, I’m trying to get in good enough shape to play both offense and defense and gain weight. How are you measuring your development? I’m keeping track of my weight gain as well as watching my numbers grow in the weight room. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I occasionally work with trainers for recovery and workouts, but most of my workouts come from my football coaches and myself. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I reached 9 feet, 8 inches on my broad jump and clocked a 40-yard dash of 4.63 seconds. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Enjoy what you do and do it right.
